pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9-11 (Upper KS2/Grades 4-6): complete vs incomplete metamorphosis. COMPLETE: egg → larva → pupa → adult (butterflies, beetles, flies) — the larva looks nothing like the adult. INCOMPLETE: egg → nymph → adult (grasshoppers, dragonflies, crickets) — the nymph is a small version of the adult that moults as it grows, with no pupa stage.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 Y5 'Living things and their habitats' — describe the differences in the life cycles of a variety of animals, including insects.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-LS1-1 (diverse life cycles with common elements).
• Operational details — the core is a CONTRAST between two life-cycle patterns and CLASSIFYING insects into them. Two discriminating features: (a) number of stages (4 with a pupa vs 3 with no pupa) and (b) does the young resemble the adult? (nymph yes / larva no). Present the two cycles side by side; classify examples by these features. This synthesises the earlier complete-metamorphosis node with the incomplete pattern.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): describes the stages of each type on a diagram. Tier B (age 10): classifies three insects correctly (butterfly=complete; grasshopper=incomplete). Tier C (age 11): explains the two discriminating features (pupa present? young resembles adult?) and uses them to justify a classification.
bestPractices: Teach it as a CONTRAST — present both cycles side by side so the differences are salient.
Anchor classification to two discriminating features: is there a pupa? does the young resemble the adult?
Use the nymph-resembles-adult vs larva-looks-different distinction as the memorable hook.
Have children classify varied examples by feature, not by memorised lists.
Build on the prior complete-metamorphosis node, adding the incomplete pattern as the contrast.
keyRepresentations: Two side-by-side cycle diagrams (4-stage with pupa vs 3-stage without).
A nymph-vs-larva morph comparison (young like adult vs unrecognisable).
A complete/incomplete sorting bin for insect examples.
commonMisconceptions: 'All insects have a caterpillar/pupa stage' — incomplete-metamorphosis insects have neither.
'A nymph is the same as a larva' — nymphs resemble the adult; larvae do not.
'Incomplete means something is missing/wrong' — it's simply a different, complete pattern (no pupa).
'Moulting only happens in one type' — both types moult; only complete has a pupal transformation.
'The number of stages is the only difference' — the young-resembles-adult feature also distinguishes them.

learn.summary: For ages 9-11 (Upper KS2/Grades 4-6), teach complete vs incomplete insect metamorphosis as a CONTRAST between two life-cycle patterns, then have learners CLASSIFY insects using two discriminating features: (a) is there a pupa stage? and (b) does the young resemble the adult? Complete metamorphosis (butterflies, beetles, flies): egg → larva → pupa → adult, where the larva looks nothing like the adult. Incomplete metamorphosis (grasshoppers, dragonflies, crickets): egg → nymph → adult, where the nymph (in grasshoppers and crickets, for example) is typically a small version of the adult without fully developed wings that moults bigger with no pupa stage. Both patterns are complete and normal; both involve moulting. The presence or absence of a pupa is the definitive discriminator; whether the young resembles the adult is a strong supporting cue that holds for most insects but can be ambiguous in a few cases (such as the dragonfly nymph), so rely on the pupa when the two cues seem to disagree. Classification should rest on developmental features, not surface cues such as colour, wings or flight.

activities.title: Run two life cycles side by side and classify by feature
feedback: If a learner routes a grasshopper or dragonfly through a pupa stage: show the two cycles together and establish that a pupa is NOT universal — incomplete-metamorphosis insects never have one.

If a learner calls a grasshopper nymph a 'larva' or 'caterpillar': point out that a larva goes on to become a pupa before the adult (caterpillar→chrysalis→butterfly), while a nymph moults straight into the adult with no pupa. Resemblance is a helpful cue: a larva looks nothing like the adult, and a grasshopper nymph looks like a small adult (baby grasshopper→grasshopper).

If a learner sorts by adult appearance (wings, bright colour, flies): redirect to the developmental features — is there a pupa? does the young look like the adult? Treat the presence or absence of a pupa as the decisive test, with young-resembles-adult as a strong supporting cue that can be ambiguous (for example, the dragonfly's aquatic nymph looks different from the adult yet has no pupa, so it is still incomplete).
On a correct sort, prompt: 'Which feature told you — the pupa, or whether the young resembles the adult?' to confirm reasoning rather than a lucky guess.
activities.rationale: Presenting both cycles together makes the differences salient, and anchoring classification to the discriminating features — with the pupa as the decisive test — helps learners generalise to unfamiliar insects instead of memorising which species belong where. This builds on prior knowledge of complete metamorphosis by adding the incomplete pattern as the explicit contrast. Running both cycles in parallel and surfacing the deciding question on an error are concrete ways to exercise feature-based reasoning; dragging into labelled bins and a morph-tracker that shows the nymph staying recognisably like the adult while it simply moults bigger (the larva, by contrast, staying unrecognisable until the pupa) are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism visible, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y5 pupils describe the differences in the life cycles of a variety of animals, including insects.
Complete metamorphosis (holometaboly) has a pupal stage and a larva unlike the adult; incomplete metamorphosis (hemimetaboly) has nymphs resembling the adult and no pupa.
learnerActions: Lay out two life cycles in parallel. Left: a butterfly — egg, then a caterpillar (larva) that looks NOTHING like the adult, then a pupa (chrysalis), then the winged adult — four stages.
Right: a grasshopper — egg, then a nymph that already looks like a tiny wingless adult and simply moults bigger and bigger until grown — three stages, no pupa.
Track the two young side by side: note that the right-hand nymph resembles its parent the whole way, while the left-hand larva is transformed beyond recognition inside the pupa.
Sort a tray of further insects — beetle, dragonfly, fly, cricket — into COMPLETE and INCOMPLETE piles.

For each insect, ask the two deciding questions: 'Is there a pupa? Does the young look like the adult?' Use the presence or absence of a pupa as the decisive test, with young-resembles-adult as a supporting cue — and if the two seem to disagree (as can happen with the dragonfly, whose nymph looks different yet has no pupa), rely on the pupa.
When a sort is wrong, state which feature you overlooked and re-sort, checking the pupa first.
activities.intendedInsight: The two life-cycle patterns differ in linked ways — number of stages (4 with a pupa vs 3 with no pupa) and whether the young resembles the adult (larva no / nymph yes). The presence or absence of a pupa is the definitive feature for classifying any insect; whether the young resembles the adult is a strong supporting cue that works for most insects but can be ambiguous in a few cases (such as the dragonfly nymph), so lean on the pupa when the cues conflict.

activities.title: Diagram the stages and distinguish nymph from larva
feedback: If a learner treats 'incomplete' as meaning something is missing or wrong: clarify it is simply a different, complete pattern with no pupa — not a defective one.
If a learner says only one type moults: point out both types moult as they grow; only complete metamorphosis adds a pupal transformation.
If a learner says the number of stages is the only difference: add the young-resembles-adult feature as the second distinguishing cue.
activities.rationale: An annotated side-by-side comparison labels both cycles and highlights the pupa/no-pupa and nymph/larva differences clearly, supporting the vocabulary and stage-naming that underpin classification. A tap-to-reveal comparison is an optional interaction example that makes the stages explicit; this is a scaffold and does not itself exercise the classify-by-feature reasoning. Preserved as a distinct activity because it serves a different pedagogical purpose (naming and defining) from the classification task.
sourceClaims: Complete metamorphosis (holometaboly) has a pupal stage and a larva unlike the adult; incomplete metamorphosis (hemimetaboly) has nymphs resembling the adult and no pupa.
learnerActions: Label both cycles on a side-by-side diagram: the 4-stage cycle with its pupa and the 3-stage cycle without.
Reveal each stage in turn and name it (egg, larva, pupa, adult vs egg, nymph, adult).
State in your own words the two discriminating features and point to where each shows up on the diagram.

Explain the difference between a nymph and a larva: a nymph usually resembles a small adult and moults straight into the adult with no pupa; a larva looks completely different from the adult and goes through a pupa stage before becoming the adult.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can name the stages of each pattern and articulate what makes nymph and larva different, giving them the vocabulary the classification task depends on.

activities.title: Classify, sequence and transfer to tricky cases
feedback: For the dragonfly case: the deciding feature is the absence of a pupa; 'looks a bit different' is not enough to make it complete metamorphosis — this is exactly why the pupa, not resemblance, is the decisive test.

For the frog case: note that frogs are amphibians, not insects, so 'complete/incomplete metamorphosis' terms describe insect life cycles — discuss what is similar (dramatic change, no pupa) and why the insect labels do not simply carry over.
If a learner classifies unfamiliar insects unreliably or muddles nymph and larva, return them to the defining features, checking the pupa first, and re-sort.
activities.rationale: Ordered comparison and classification are assessed directly by sorting, sequencing and feature-choice tasks, while counterexamples (dragonfly nymph) and cross-group transfer (frog) reveal whether the learner holds the criteria or just remembers 'butterfly = 4 stages'. These probes expose shallow surface-cue reasoning and reinforce that the pupa is the decisive discriminator. The frog item is cross-group transfer; the insect-specific metamorphosis labels do not map cleanly onto amphibians, so it is best used as a discussion of boundaries rather than a forced classification.

learnerActions: Sort insects into complete vs incomplete and, separately, put each cycle's stages into the correct order.
Choose which single feature best tells the two types apart and justify why (the pupa stage is present only in complete metamorphosis, so it is the most reliable discriminator).

Tackle a tricky counterexample: a young dragonfly (nymph) lives underwater and looks somewhat different from the flying adult — does that make it complete metamorphosis? Explain (it still has NO pupa, so it is incomplete, which is why the pupa is the decisive feature).
Transfer across groups: a frog goes tadpole → frog with no pupa, but the tadpole looks nothing like the frog. Decide whether this is like complete, incomplete, or neither, and explain your reasoning.
State the one stage a complete-metamorphosis insect has that an incomplete one never has.
activities.intendedInsight: Relational understanding means applying the defining criteria consistently — treating the pupa as decisive and resemblance as a supporting cue — including in cases where a nymph looks a bit different or where an animal is outside the insect group, rather than leaning on a single cue or a memorised butterfly cycle.

constraints: Classification must rest on developmental features, not surface cues such as wings, colour or flight. The presence or absence of a pupa is the definitive discriminator; whether the young resembles the adult is a strong supporting cue that holds for most insects but can be ambiguous (e.g. the dragonfly nymph looks different from the adult yet has no pupa, so it is incomplete). When the two cues disagree, the pupa decides.
A labelled or tap-to-reveal side-by-side diagram supports naming and vocabulary but does not by itself exercise the classify-by-feature reasoning; pair it with an actual sorting/justification task.

Multiple-choice, ordering and sorting formats can be used during teaching as well as for assessment, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the independent justification ('how can you tell?') that shows relational understanding — require learners to state the deciding feature.
Both metamorphosis types involve moulting; only complete metamorphosis adds a pupal transformation. 'Incomplete' means a different complete pattern, not a defective or missing one.

In insects such as grasshoppers and crickets, the nymph resembles the adult from the start and grows larger by moulting, with wing buds gradually developing; do not describe or depict these nymphs as beginning unlike the adult and only later coming to resemble it — that would blur the nymph/larva distinction. Some nymphs, such as the aquatic dragonfly nymph, look noticeably different from the adult, yet they still have no pupa, so they are still incomplete metamorphosis.

The frog example is outside the insect group; use it as a boundary/transfer discussion, not as an insect-classification item, since the complete/incomplete insect terms do not straightforwardly apply to amphibians.

Interaction examples (side-by-side cycle rings, a morph-tracker, drag-to-bin sorting, error-triggered deciding questions) are optional ways to make the contrast concrete, not mandatory mechanisms; the same learning can be achieved with paper diagrams, cut-out cards and spoken justification.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The three cited sources are marked verified:false in the row; treat curriculum alignment and the holometaboly/hemimetaboly definitions as unconfirmed here.

The original asserted that side-by-side manipulation teaches the contrast 'in a way a static diagram can't' and that a fixed comparison 'is better shown and sorted than discussed'. These are catalog-fit claims, not established comparative-efficacy findings; softened to scoped affordances. A static diagram can still teach the stages and vocabulary, and discussion is useful for justification and transfer.

Corrected an internal contradiction: one rationale described a morph-tracker showing the nymph 'gradually coming to resemble the adult', which clashes with the taught point that the nymph resembles the adult the whole way; reworded so the nymph stays recognisably adult-like while only the larva remains unrecognisable until the pupa.

The two discriminating features can conflict: the dragonfly's aquatic nymph does not clearly resemble the adult, yet the dragonfly is incomplete because it has no pupa. The guidance now states the pupa is the decisive discriminator and resemblance a strong but fallible supporting cue, applied consistently across the summary, activity 0, the dragonfly counterexample in activity 2, and the constraints. This resolution should be checked against a verified entomology source.

The frog transfer item: the source treats it as a cross-group case. Flagged because insect metamorphosis labels do not cleanly extend to amphibians; kept as a boundary discussion rather than a required classification.

probeDeeper: 'You sorted the dragonfly as incomplete. Which feature told you — the way the young looks, or the pupa? Explain.'

'A young dragonfly (a nymph) lives underwater and looks quite different from the flying adult — does that make it complete metamorphosis? Why or why not?' (tricky counterexample: nymph that looks somewhat different but still has NO pupa)
'What is the one stage that a complete-metamorphosis insect has that an incomplete one never has?'
'A frog: tadpole → frog, no pupa, but the tadpole looks nothing like the frog. Is that like complete, incomplete, or neither?' (cross-group transfer)
assess.correctAnswer: The butterfly goes through COMPLETE metamorphosis (egg → larva → pupa → adult), where the young (larva) looks completely different from the adult and the body is rebuilt in a pupa. The grasshopper goes through INCOMPLETE metamorphosis (egg → nymph → adult), where the nymph already resembles a small adult and there is no pupa. Beetle = complete; fly = complete; dragonfly = incomplete. You tell them apart by two things: does the young look like a mini-adult (incomplete) or totally different (complete), and is there a pupa stage (only in complete)?

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks ALL insects go through complete metamorphosis — assumes every insect has a caterpillar/larva and a pupa
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast two life cycles side by side: butterfly (young totally different, has pupa) vs grasshopper (young is a mini-adult, no pupa). Establish that a pupa is NOT universal.
errorPatterns.distractor: Both the butterfly and the grasshopper go through a pupa stage
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Puts the grasshopper/dragonfly through a pupa stage; can't accept a young insect that already looks like the adult

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses 'nymph' and 'larva' — treats them as the same, missing that a nymph resembles the adult but a larva does not
errorPatterns.nextMove: Define by resemblance: larva = looks nothing like the adult (caterpillar→butterfly); nymph = looks like a small adult (baby grasshopper→grasshopper). Match the term to whether the young resembles the adult.
errorPatterns.distractor: A grasshopper nymph is the same as a caterpillar larva
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: calls a grasshopper nymph a larva/caterpillar; can't state the resemblance difference

errorPatterns.pattern: Classifies by surface features (has wings / is colourful / flies) instead of the young-vs-adult resemblance and pupa criteria
errorPatterns.nextMove: Redirect to the two defining questions (does the young look like the adult? is there a pupa?) for each insect; ignore adult appearance. Use those questions as the sole sort rule.
errorPatterns.distractor: You can tell the type from whether the adult has wings or bright colours
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sorts the beetle/dragonfly/fly by looks or flight rather than by their developmental features; gets them wrong

responseLevels.gap: Thinks all insects have a caterpillar and pupa, or sorts by adult appearance; can't distinguish the two types.
responseLevels.full: Classifies by the defining criteria (young resembles adult? pupa present?), sorts unfamiliar insects correctly, distinguishes nymph from larva, AND transfers the reasoning to a tricky case (dragonfly nymph, or frog) — relational understanding rather than a memorised butterfly cycle.
responseLevels.partial: Knows butterfly = complete and grasshopper = incomplete and can name the stages, but classifies new insects unreliably — leans on one cue or muddles nymph and larva, without consistently using both defining features.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A butterfly and a grasshopper grow up very differently. A butterfly is a caterpillar, then a chrysalis, then an adult. A baby grasshopper hatches already looking like a tiny grasshopper and just gets bigger. Which one goes through 'complete' metamorphosis and which 'incomplete'? Sort these three — beetle, dragonfly, fly — into the right type too, and explain how you can tell.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the contrast classifies by the DEFINING features — does the young resemble the adult, and is there a pupa — and applies them to new insects. A child with a shallow grasp thinks all insects have a caterpillar/pupa, or classifies by surface cues (has wings, is pretty) rather than the young-vs-adult resemblance. The second-tier sorting of unfamiliar insects (beetle/dragonfly/fly) plus 'how can you tell' exposes whether they hold the criteria or just remember butterfly = 4 stages.
